result.summary: Pan boasts of his piping and challenges Apollo, and the mountain Tmolus judges Apollo the winner. Midas alone objects, so Apollo gives him ass's ears. Midas hides them, but his barber whispers the secret into a hole in the ground and reeds grow there and repeat it on the wind.

scenes.title: Midas follows Pan
scenes.summary: After abandoning riches, Midas lives in the woods and follows Pan, but he is still foolish.
scenes.stakes: Midas risks further harm from his own dull judgment.

scenes.title: The contest on Tmolus
scenes.summary: Pan plays his reeds and Apollo plays his lyre before Tmolus. Tmolus and all but Midas favour Apollo.
scenes.stakes: Pan risks defeat in a contest with a god; Midas risks the anger of Apollo by condemning the verdict.

scenes.title: Midas gets ass's ears
scenes.summary: Apollo gives Midas the ears of an ass as punishment, and Midas hides them under a purple turban.
scenes.stakes: Midas faces public shame over his disfigurement.

scenes.title: The barber and the reeds
scenes.summary: The barber cannot keep the secret, whispers it into a hole and buries it. Reeds grow there and betray it in the wind.
scenes.stakes: The barber risks punishment for revealing the secret; Midas's secret is in danger of exposure.

alias_notes.explanation: Apollo is called Delian from Delos, his birthplace.

notable_quotes.reason: The reeds repeat the buried secret, the famous ending of the Midas ears tale.

analysis.text: Midas's folly shows poor judgment, now in matters of art, and the gods punish it fittingly with a visible mark.
The secret that cannot be kept shows that hidden truths will out, even through nature.

legacy.text: The phrase "Midas has ass's ears" and the whispering reeds became a proverbial image for an unkeepable secret.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's version shares its barber-and-reeds secret with older folk tales found in many cultures.

language_notes.text: 'As before' recalls Midas's foolish wish for the golden touch, which nearly starved him until he washed it away in the river Pactolus.
'Reeds joined with wax' describes the panpipes, made of reeds of different lengths fastened together with wax.
Tmolus clears the trees from his ears so he can hear properly; as a mountain god, trees grow on his head.
The plectrum is a small pick used to strike or pluck the strings of a lyre.
'Delian God' means Apollo, called Delian because he was born on the island of Delos.
A turban here is a wrapped headcloth, used to hide the ears; purple suggests royal rank.

context_notes.text: Pan is the god of flocks, shepherds and wild places, often shown playing reed pipes.
Tmolus is a mountain in Lydia, Asia Minor, near Sardis, the Lydian capital. It is also personified as the god of the mountain.
Laurel was sacred to Apollo, and Parnassus was a mountain sacred to him and the Muses. Tyrian purple was a costly dye.

literary_notes.text: The mountain is a god with hair and temples, crowned with oak and acorns, so the landscape itself judges the contest.
Apollo's elegant dress and pose show him as the refined master of art, in contrast to rustic Pan.
The ass's ears make Midas's dull judgment visible; his body is marked as his mind was.
The servant's buried secret is carried by the wind through the reeds, so the attempt at concealment becomes the means of exposure.
